Prior authorization checks that applicable Medicare coverage, payment and coding requirements are met before the item is delivered. ## How items are selected CMS keeps a Master List of DMEPOS items that may require prior authorization or a face-to-face encounter with a written order before delivery. The list is updated at least once a year based on items with patterns of unnecessary utilization. Items on the Required Prior Authorization List are chosen by evaluating DMEPOS categories for problematic billing trends. Recent additions include orthoses, power mobility devices, pressure reducing support surfaces, lower limb prosthetics and pneumatic compression devices. Selected items usually start in some geographic regions and then expand nationwide.

Nurse practitioners, clinical nurse specialists and certified nurse midwives may perform initial visits where state law permits and collaboration and supervision requirements are met. Office and outpatient: physicians and qualified nonphysician practitioners choose a new or established patient visit code (99201-99215) based on visit complexity and the patient relationship. A new patient is one who has not received professional services from the physician or physician group practice within the previous 3 years.

Critical Access Hospital Method II: appropriate new or established visit codes (99201-99215) are reported on type of bill 85X with revenue codes 96X, 97X or 98X for physicians and nonphysician practitioners with reassigned billing rights.

Rural Health Clinics and Federally Qualified Health Centers: consultation codes were discontinued in favor of office visit codes (99201-99215) and nursing facility codes (99304-99306) as appropriate.

final_text:
**Claim 1478014 has a low denial risk: 11.3%. The validation-set average is 18.1%.** This is an outpatient claim for HCPCS 90935 with principal diagnosis N18.4. The denial label in this project is synthetic. It was built from risk rules, so the score is the probability of that constructed label. It is not a prediction of a real payer decision.

**Why the score is low**
- The billed code, 90935, is the main driver. It cuts the odds of denial by about 24% (odds × 0.76).
- The other features have small effects. The largest are a few fields with no value (NOT_APPLICABLE). One example is the billing NPI field, which lowers the odds slightly. Another is the line number, which raises them slightly.
- Diagnosis N18.4 adds a small push upward (odds × 1.03).
- Several of these fields aren't in the project's data dictionary, so I won't say what they mean here.

**What a billing team could check**
My policy search found nothing on 90935 or on this diagnosis. The policy set only covers consultation codes, CPAP, and DMEPOS prior authorization. So the checks below are general good practice, not project rules:
- The code matches the documented service.
- The diagnosis supports the service.
- The provider and billing identifiers are complete, since several of those fields are blank on this claim.
- The payer's own rules have been reviewed.
